basic_info.basic_info: Understanding the partner's preferences means gathering, before the date, their likes/dislikes, allergies, physical activity level, and dietary constraints, and using this as the foundation on which the whole course is built. Unlike the 'budget appropriateness' factor (which calibrates how much to spend) or 'novelty/variety' (which calibrates stimulation), this factor is about content fit: making sure every element of the course is compatible with, and ideally delightful to, this specific person rather than a generic 'good date'. Its mechanism is signaling responsiveness and removing friction/risk, not spectacle.

rationale.psychology: The core mechanism is Perceived Partner Responsiveness (PPR; Reis, Clark, & Holmes, 2004; roots in Reis & Shaver, 1988). People feel closer and more satisfied when they perceive a partner as understanding, validating, and caring for their needs and preferences. Planning a date around someone's actual tastes is a concrete behavioral demonstration of all three components (understanding = 'you know me', validation = 'my preferences matter', caring = 'I acted on them'), one of the strongest predictors of attraction and relationship quality. Second, it functions as costly/honest signaling (Zahavi; costly signaling theory in evolutionary psychology): the time and mental effort to learn and accommodate preferences is a non-salvageable investment that partners appreciate more than raw money, because effort is hard to fake (gift-giving research finds mental effort and non-recoverable cost drive perceived thoughtfulness). Third, it prevents strong negative peak experiences: the peak-end rule (Kahneman) means one aversive moment (an allergic reaction, an inedible dish, an activity beyond someone's fitness, a triggered phobia) can dominate the entire memory of the date, so screening these out protects the affective trace. Fourth, matching activity level supports self-expansion (Aron & Aron, 1986) safely: an arousing shared activity boosts attraction only if it stays within the partner's comfort/ability band; beyond it, arousal is experienced as threat, not excitement. Fifth, knowing/being-known and reciprocal self-disclosure (Aron et al., 1997, the '36 questions') deepen intimacy; asking about preferences is itself an intimacy-building disclosure exchange, not merely logistics.

application.how_to_apply: 1) Gather preferences naturally in conversation before the date: weave in questions like 'anything you don't eat or can't have?', 'are you more active-outdoorsy or a relaxed-cafe person?', 'coffee, tea, or neither?'. Frame it as caring, not interrogation. 2) Always explicitly confirm allergies and hard dietary constraints (vegetarian/vegan/halal/kosher/lactose/gluten/alcohol) as a safety gate, and pick venues that can accommodate them; check the menu online in advance and, for severe allergies, call the venue about their allergen protocol. 3) Calibrate the activity to their physical activity level and mobility: don't plan a 10km hike or a standing-only event for someone sedentary or with joint issues; offer a lighter alternative. 4) Build the course on at least one confirmed 'like' as an anchor (a cuisine they love, a hobby, a favorite genre) so there is a guaranteed hit. 5) Avoid known dislikes and dealbreakers entirely (spicy food, horror, crowds, seafood smell, etc.). 6) Keep a low-key backup that still fits their profile in case the primary plan fails (weather, closure). 7) Where unsure, ask directly rather than guess on high-stakes items (allergies, alcohol, venue formality). 8) Show your work lightly on the day ('I remembered you said you love X, so...') so the responsiveness is perceived, not just quietly performed.
application.common_mistakes: Projecting your own taste onto them ('I love this place so they will too') instead of building on their preferences. Treating dietary constraints as mere preferences and picking a steakhouse for a vegetarian, or worse, ignoring an allergy, which is a safety failure that can wreck the date via the peak-end effect. Over-surveying: turning preference-gathering into a cold questionnaire or demanding a full profile up front, which feels transactional and kills spontaneity. Guessing on high-stakes items rather than confirming. Over-accommodating to the point of erasing yourself, so the date has no personality or shared discovery. Mismatching activity level: booking an ambitious physical activity to seem exciting when the partner is not equipped for it, converting self-expansion arousal into anxiety. Announcing every accommodation so loudly it reads as fishing for credit rather than genuine care.
application.examples: 1) Early texting reveals she is lactose-intolerant and loves Korean food but dislikes very spicy dishes; the course becomes a mild, dairy-free-friendly Korean restaurant (menu confirmed in advance) followed by a sorbet dessert bar instead of ice cream, quietly signaling 'I listened.' 2) A partner mentions they are not very active and tire easily; instead of a bike-rental river course, the plan is a short flat riverside walk plus a cozy cafe with seating, keeping the pleasant novelty of a new place without physical strain. 3) He casually says he doesn't drink; the plan swaps the default wine bar for a specialty coffee roastery and a dessert cafe, removing awkward pressure around alcohol while still feeling intentional and warm.

evidence.evidence: Psychological basis: Reis, Clark, & Holmes (2004) on Perceived Partner Responsiveness; Reis & Shaver (1988) intimacy model. Self-expansion: Aron & Aron (1986); Aron et al. (1997) '36 questions'. Peak-end rule: Kahneman et al. (1993). Costly/honest signaling and effort-over-money in gifts: Costly signaling theory in evolutionary psychology, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costly_signaling_theory_in_evolutionary_psychology ; gift-giving as commitment signal, https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1090513818300552 ; commitment signals in relationships, https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1090513815000525 .
